Redox Isomerization/(3 + 2) Allenoate Annulation by Auto-
Tandem Phosphine Catalysis
Jeremy T. Maddigan-Wyatt,
[a]
Mitchell T. Blyth,
[b]
Jhi Ametovski,
[a]
Michelle L. Coote,
[b]
Joel F. Hooper,*
[a]
and David W. Lupton*
[a]
Abstract: A phosphine-catalyzed approach to pyrrolines has
been developed that involves two mechanistically unlinked
catalytic processes. The first involves the redox isomerization
of amino crotonates to provide access to aliphatic tosyl
imines, which then engage in a (3 + 2) annulation with various
allenoates. The reaction shows generality, with 24 examples
established, along with a low yielding and moderately
enantioselective variant. Mechanistic studies indicate that the
viability of the process is linked to the selection of catalysts
with similar propensity to add to the two coupling partners.
Reactions mediated by a single catalyst, in a single catalytic
cycle, are ubiquitous in organic synthesis, and have allowed a
number of privileged catalyst classes to be developed. While
they continue to feature prominently in reaction discovery,
tandem catalytic approaches, featuring either one or multiple
catalysts, have increasingly drawn attention.
[1]
Commonly these
processes exploit two or more catalysts working cooperatively
to access novel reactivity in reactions that can be defined as
orthogonal tandem catalysis.
[2]
An alternate approach draws
upon the breadth of reactivity available from a single catalyst
allowing transformations via multiple mechanistically distinct
processes in so-called auto-tandem catalytic reactions.
[3]
In
contrast to cascade catalytic processes, in which reactions of
multiple intermediates in a single catalytic cycle are achieved,
mediation of mechanistically distinct events in auto-tandem
catalysis in principle allows any number of isolated reactions to
be coupled. For example, in 2004 Evans communicated the
synthesis of cyclopentenone 1 via assisted auto-tandem
catalysis using a Rh[I] species.
[4]
In the first cycle allylic allylation
(Cycle A) produces 4 which, upon increasing the reaction
temperature, reengages with the catalyst to provide the
Pauson-Khand adduct 1 (Figure 1A).
While auto-tandem catalysis involving transition metals (i. e.
Figure 1A) are increasingly established,
[3,4]
related approaches in
organocatalysis are less so. In previous studies from our group
we demonstrated that the Lewis and Brønsted basicity of a
single N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) catalyst can be exploited in
the synthesis of 6 by auto-tandem catalysis (Figure 1B).
[5]
Building upon these studies we considered opportunities
presented by phosphines.
[6]
Phosphines are some of the first
organocatalysts,
[7]
and are capable of mediating a diverse array
of normal and reverse polarity reactions. In addition to
annulative reactions, we were drawn to their capacity to
achieve redox isomerization such as in the conversion of
alkynoates (i. e. 7) to dienoates (i. e. 8) (Figure 1C).
[8]
Such
isomerizations are unusual in Lewis base organocatalysis,

Specifically, we postulated that if
amino crotonates such as 10 could undergo a related redox
isomerization then this would give aliphatic imines such as 11
(Figure 1C). Such species have established utility, but can be
challenging to prepare and isolate due to issues with hydrolytic
stability. Based on the known isomerizations of alkynes and
allenes, the proposed isomerization (i. e. 10!11) appears
plausible, although related reactions of simple Michael accept-
ors are unknown. In the second catalytic event the phosphine
would mediate annulation of the previously formed imine 11
with an appropriate allenoate 12, building upon chemistry
discovered by Lu,
[10]
and developed by Kwon,
[11]
Shi,
[12]
and
others,
[13,14]
to give pyrroline 13. Herein, we report the outcome
of our studies on this topic with the development of a redox
isomerization/(3 + 2) annulation by auto-tandem phosphine
catalysis (Figure 1D). To the best of our knowledge this is the
first report of phosphine catalyzed redox isomerization of a
simple Michael acceptor, and provides a new route to pyrrolines
derived from less common aliphatic imine precursors.
[13]
We commenced our investigations by examining the
proposed redox isomerization aspect of the design using amino
crotonate 10 a. When subjected to a series of known phosphine
organocatalysts, rather than forming the desired imine 11 a,
imidazolidine 14 a was isolated (Figure 2A). The formation of
14 a suggests the intermediacy of the targeted imine, which
then undergoes annulation with a second equivalent of amine
10 a to give the observed product. Further supporting this

With the viability of the postulated redox isomerization
established we turned our attention to the pyrroline synthesis
(Table 1). Studies commenced by examining the coupling of
amino crotonate 10 a with allenoate 12 a using the same family
of catalysts introduced in the previous study (Table 1, entries 1–
6). Mirroring the trends observed previously we found that the
catalysts successful in the redox isomerization also gave the
expected pyrroline 13 a in yields between 23 and 40 % yield
(Table entries 1–3), although accompanied by a significant
amount of an alternate annulation product, pyrrole 15 a. This
material presumably forms by competitive addition of the
phosphine to allenoate 12 a and union with the amino
crotonate 10 a partner without redox isomerization. This
reaction is mechanistically related to transformations reported
by Sasai with related oxygen containing heterocycles.
[15]

complete selectivity for the formation of pyrrole 13 a could be
achieved using dichloroethane (Table 1, entry 8), although the
isolated yield decreased. While isolation of compound 13 a from
pyrrole 15 a was challenging, it was achievable, hence the less
selective, but higher yielding, conditions exploiting dichloro-
methane as solvent were viewed as optimal, providing pyrolline
13 a in 53 % isolated yield with 9 % of pyrrole 15 a (Table 1,
entry 7). While modest, this correlates to an average of 73 %
yield for each of the two catalytic events required to make
pyrolline 13 a.
Studies into the scope of the transformation commenced by
modifying the amine partner to gain an appreciation for the
generality of the redox isomerization (Table 2). The reaction was
found to be insensitive to alternate esters with pyrrolines 13 b–f
formed in 59–77 % yield. In all cases small amounts of the
pyrrole by-product 15 formed which could be isolated from 13
by column chromatography. Phenyl ketone containing sub-
strates were suitable, with 13 g produced in only slightly
decreased yield, while nitriles gave the corresponding pyrroline
13 h in a low yield of 17 %. The nature of the amine protection
was examined with electron-rich and electron-poor sulphona-
mides tolerated (to form 13 i and j), although the nosyl
containing 13 k formed in only 39 % isolated yield. In all cases
complete diastereoselectivity for the cis-adduct was observed,
as it was for all reactions in this study, and as is common for
such annulations.
[10–14]
Next attention was directed to the allenoate partner. Initially
this was modified by examining alternate electron withdrawing
functionality. While various esters were compatible with the
reaction (to give 13 l–p) switching to more electron-withdraw-
ing aryl ketones presumably favored direct addition of the
phosphine to the allenone (increase of ΔΔG
�
) thus giving the
pyrrole product 15 y. Changing the substituent within the
allenoate was examined next. Switching from a phenyl to a
methyl or ethyl group led to a moderate decrease in yield (i. e.
13 a formed in 53 % yield while 13 q–s were produced in yields
from 40 to 46 %). Larger alkyl groups, such as iso-propyl or
cyclohexyl, gave the expected pyrroline products 13 t and 13 u
in 72 and 53 % yield respectively. The phenyl group was
replaced by a para-MeO aryl or a 1- or 2-napthyl (13 v–x) and
the reaction occurred with a moderate decrease to reaction
yield. The later structure, 13 x, was analysed by single crystal x-
ray diffraction to allow confirmation of the stereochemical
assignment.
[17]
Finally, deletion of the R
1
substituent in 12 led
only to formation of the undesired pyrrole (i. e. 15) by-product
in modest yield.
An enantioselective version of the reaction was investigated
using a range of chiral phosphines (see Table Supporting
Information-3 for details). While highly enantioselective (3 + 2)
annulations with electron deficient olefins are well established
6
annulations of imines, particularly aliphatic imines, are known
to be more challenging.
[14]
Unfortunately, after preliminary
optimization only phosphepine D3 – a catalyst derived from
structures of Marinetti for (3 + 2) annulations of imines
[14a]
– was
viable. However, unfortunately the reaction only provided
pyrroline 13 a with a modest yield and low levels of
enantioselectivity (Scheme 1). While these studies demonstrate
the viability of the enantioselective variant of this reaction,

To examine the inherent reactivity of the pyrroline products
derivatizations were performed (Figure 3A). Thiolate addition
could be achieved without ester cleavage to give 16 m in 63 %
yield as a 2 : 1 mixture of diastereomers. While hydrogenation
proceeded with some diastereoselectivity to give tetrahydropyr-
role 17 t in 72 % yield as a 2 : 1 mixture of diastereoisomers.
As discussed previously the key to the viability of this
reaction is the use of a catalyst that can undergo addition to
both allenoate and crotonate with similar activation energies,
thus allowing both catalytic cycles to operate in concert. If we
consider Cycle A (Figure 3B) we propose that the 1,4-addition
into the amino crotonate occurs to give enolate 18, which
following catalyst elimination gives enamine 19 and ultimately
imine 11 a. Concurrently, addition of the phosphine catalyst to
allenoate 12 b gives rise to 1,3-dipole 20 which undergoes
union with imine 11 a to give 21 then, following annulation,
ylide 22. Elimination of the catalyst then furnishes the pyrroline
13 b. The events in Cycle B are drawn from previously reported
mechanistic studies in related phosphine (3 + 2) annulations.
[18]
Methods to assemble complex fine chemicals are becoming
increasingly sophisticated. While much effort has been directed
to the development of multicatalyst systems to access new
reactivity patterns,
[2]
this approach by definition exploits more
than one catalyst, potentially decreasing efficiency, and requir-
ing catalyst compatibility. By exploiting a single catalyst, in an
auto-tandem catalytic process, novel reactivity can be accessed,
while avoiding these limitations. In addition, the reaction design
can draw upon the wealth of knowledge often associated with
a single catalyst family. Herein, we have developed an auto-
tandem catalytic approach that exploits a novel redox isomer-
ization with an established (3 + 2) annulation. This pair of
reactions exploits the diversity of transformations available with
phosphine catalysts. While successful this study highlights some
of the challenges associated with the development of auto-
tandem catalytic reactions.

Redox Isomerization/(3 + 2) Allenoate Annulation by Auto-
Tandem Phosphine Catalysis
Jeremy T. Maddigan-Wyatt,
[a]
Mitchell T. Blyth,
[b]
Jhi Ametovski,
[a]
Michelle L. Coote,
[b]
Joel F. Hooper,*
[a]
and David W. Lupton*
[a]
Abstract: A phosphine-catalyzed approach to pyrrolines has
been developed that involves two mechanistically unlinked
catalytic processes. The first involves the redox isomerization
of amino crotonates to provide access to aliphatic tosyl
imines, which then engage in a (3 + 2) annulation with various
allenoates. The reaction shows generality, with 24 examples
established, along with a low yielding and moderately
enantioselective variant. Mechanistic studies indicate that the
viability of the process is linked to the selection of catalysts
with similar propensity to add to the two coupling partners.
Reactions mediated by a single catalyst, in a single catalytic
cycle, are ubiquitous in organic synthesis, and have allowed a
number of privileged catalyst classes to be developed. While
they continue to feature prominently in reaction discovery,
tandem catalytic approaches, featuring either one or multiple
catalysts, have increasingly drawn attention.
[1]
Commonly these
processes exploit two or more catalysts working cooperatively
to access novel reactivity in reactions that can be defined as
orthogonal tandem catalysis.
[2]
An alternate approach draws
upon the breadth of reactivity available from a single catalyst
allowing transformations via multiple mechanistically distinct
processes in so-called auto-tandem catalytic reactions.
[3]
In
contrast to cascade catalytic processes, in which reactions of
multiple intermediates in a single catalytic cycle are achieved,
mediation of mechanistically distinct events in auto-tandem
catalysis in principle allows any number of isolated reactions to
be coupled. For example, in 2004 Evans communicated the
synthesis of cyclopentenone 1 via assisted auto-tandem
catalysis using a Rh[I] species.
[4]
In the first cycle allylic allylation
(Cycle A) produces 4 which, upon increasing the reaction
temperature, reengages with the catalyst to provide the
Pauson-Khand adduct 1 (Figure 1A).
While auto-tandem catalysis involving transition metals (i. e.
Figure 1A) are increasingly established,
[3,4]
related approaches in
organocatalysis are less so. In previous studies from our group
we demonstrated that the Lewis and Brønsted basicity of a
single N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) catalyst can be exploited in
the synthesis of 6 by auto-tandem catalysis (Figure 1B).
[5]
Building upon these studies we considered opportunities
presented by phosphines.
[6]
Phosphines are some of the first
organocatalysts,
[7]
and are capable of mediating a diverse array
of normal and reverse polarity reactions. In addition to
annulative reactions, we were drawn to their capacity to
achieve redox isomerization such as in the conversion of
alkynoates (i. e. 7) to dienoates (i. e. 8) (Figure 1C).
[8]
Such
isomerizations are unusual in Lewis base organocatalysis,

Specifically, we postulated that if
amino crotonates such as 10 could undergo a related redox
isomerization then this would give aliphatic imines such as 11
(Figure 1C). Such species have established utility, but can be
challenging to prepare and isolate due to issues with hydrolytic
stability. Based on the known isomerizations of alkynes and
allenes, the proposed isomerization (i. e. 10!11) appears
plausible, although related reactions of simple Michael accept-
ors are unknown. In the second catalytic event the phosphine
would mediate annulation of the previously formed imine 11
with an appropriate allenoate 12, building upon chemistry
discovered by Lu,
[10]
and developed by Kwon,
[11]
Shi,
[12]
and
others,
[13,14]

of our studies on this topic with the development of a redox
isomerization/(3 + 2) annulation by auto-tandem phosphine
catalysis (Figure 1D). To the best of our knowledge this is the
first report of phosphine catalyzed redox isomerization of a
simple Michael acceptor, and provides a new route to pyrrolines
derived from less common aliphatic imine precursors.
[13]
We commenced our investigations by examining the
proposed redox isomerization aspect of the design using amino
crotonate 10 a. When subjected to a series of known phosphine
organocatalysts, rather than forming the desired imine 11 a,
imidazolidine 14 a was isolated (Figure 2A). The formation of
14 a suggests the intermediacy of the targeted imine, which
then undergoes annulation with a second equivalent of amine
10 a to give the observed product. Further supporting this

Studies into the scope of the transformation commenced by
modifying the amine partner to gain an appreciation for the
generality of the redox isomerization (Table 2). The reaction was
found to be insensitive to alternate esters with pyrrolines 13 b–f
formed in 59–77 % yield. In all cases small amounts of the
pyrrole by-product 15 formed which could be isolated from 13
by column chromatography. Phenyl ketone containing sub-
strates were suitable, with 13 g produced in only slightly
decreased yield, while nitriles gave the corresponding pyrroline
13 h in a low yield of 17 %. The nature of the amine protection
was examined with electron-rich and electron-poor sulphona-
mides tolerated (to form 13 i and j), although the nosyl
containing 13 k formed in only 39 % isolated yield. In all cases
complete diastereoselectivity for the cis-adduct was observed,
as it was for all reactions in this study, and as is common for
such annulations.
[10–14]
Next attention was directed to the allenoate partner. Initially
this was modified by examining alternate electron withdrawing
functionality. While various esters were compatible with the
reaction (to give 13 l–p) switching to more electron-withdraw-

phosphine to the allenone (increase of ΔΔG

from 40 to 46 %). Larger alkyl groups, such as iso-propyl or
cyclohexyl, gave the expected pyrroline products 13 t and 13 u
in 72 and 53 % yield respectively. The phenyl group was
replaced by a para-MeO aryl or a 1- or 2-napthyl (13 v–x) and
the reaction occurred with a moderate decrease to reaction
yield. The later structure, 13 x, was analysed by single crystal x-

both allenoate and crotonate with similar activation energies,
thus allowing both catalytic cycles to operate in concert. If we
consider Cycle A (Figure 3B) we propose that the 1,4-addition
into the amino crotonate occurs to give enolate 18, which
following catalyst elimination gives enamine 19 and ultimately
imine 11 a. Concurrently, addition of the phosphine catalyst to
allenoate 12 b gives rise to 1,3-dipole 20 which undergoes
union with imine 11 a to give 21 then, following annulation,
ylide 22. Elimination of the catalyst then furnishes the pyrroline
13 b. The events in Cycle B are drawn from previously reported
mechanistic studies in related phosphine (3 + 2) annulations.
[18]

increasingly sophisticated. While much effort has been directed
to the development of multicatalyst systems to access new
reactivity patterns,

than one catalyst, potentially decreasing efficiency, and requir-
ing catalyst compatibility. By exploiting a single catalyst, in an
auto-tandem catalytic process, novel reactivity can be accessed,
while avoiding these limitations. In addition, the reaction design
can draw upon the wealth of knowledge often associated with
a single catalyst family. Herein, we have developed an auto-
tandem catalytic approach that exploits a novel redox isomer-
ization with an established (3 + 2) annulation. This pair of
reactions exploits the diversity of transformations available with
phosphine catalysts. While successful this study highlights some
of the challenges associated with the development of auto-
tandem catalytic reactions.
